prompt.brief: Design a collaborative ML experiment-tracking service that records parameters, metrics, code/data/environment lineage, artifacts, and evaluation results so runs can be compared and reproduced.
successSignals: Define projects, runs, parameters, time-series metrics, source/code/data/environment lineage, artifacts, tags, comparisons, and lifecycle states.
Keep high-frequency logging append-only and resumable; separate metadata/query indexes from large artifact storage and enforce quotas/cardinality.
Support framework SDKs, offline buffering, run finalization, immutable versions, reproducible environment capture, and artifact integrity checks.
Explain tenant access, secret redaction, deletion/retention, concurrent logging, retries, outage recovery, observability, and local buffering.

functional: Create projects/runs, log parameters and metrics, upload artifacts, capture lineage, finalize runs, and compare/search runs.
Support dashboards, charts, tags, framework SDKs, resumable uploads, artifact download, run notes, and model-registration handoff.
Make logging idempotent, preserve append-only history, support retention/deletion, access controls, export, and recovery after agent disconnects.
nonFunctional: Acknowledge metric batches quickly and make run metadata searchable while large artifact uploads remain asynchronous.
Scale to 100k active runs, 1M metric points per second, and large artifacts without a single hot key or unbounded synchronous work.
Do not lose committed state; make retries and duplicate events safe.
Degrade safely when downstream workers, caches, or external dependencies fail.
scaleAssumptions: 100k active runs, 1M metric points/second, and petabytes of artifacts
Partition by the primary tenant, user, item, or geographic key and isolate hot partitions.
Keep serving state bounded; retain raw events or durable records for replay and auditing.

deepDives.title: Consistency and idempotency
points: Keep the Collaborative ML experiment-tracking service commit authoritative; let derived projections converge with visible version and freshness.
Use idempotency keys, conditional Collaborative ML experiment-tracking service writes, event IDs, and versions so retries and replay are safe.
Return Collaborative ML experiment-tracking service version and observedAt so clients can reason about freshness.

deepDives.title: Partitioning and hot keys
points: Partition Collaborative ML experiment-tracking service by its primary read and write keys, then isolate hot tenants, users, items, or regions.
Bound Collaborative ML experiment-tracking service work with backpressure and queue isolation so one hot key cannot dominate the cluster.
Keep a replay or reconciliation path for Collaborative ML experiment-tracking service projection drift and partial failures.

deepDives.title: Failure and recovery
points: Serve the last acceptable Collaborative ML experiment-tracking service projection or an explicit degraded response when workers fail.
Retain durable Collaborative ML experiment-tracking service records for replay and make each downstream effect independently retryable.
Measure Collaborative ML experiment-tracking service latency, backlog, freshness, error rate, and correctness drift.

tradeoffs.title: Strong consistency versus throughput
tradeoffs.recommendation: Strongly protect the business commit and use versioned eventual projections for high-volume reads.
tradeoffs.caution: Making every derived read synchronous increases coordination and tail latency.

tradeoffs.title: Push versus pull processing
tradeoffs.recommendation: Push bounded events to workers and pull durable snapshots on reads or recovery.
tradeoffs.caution: Unbounded fanout or full scans make bursts and hot keys expensive.

tradeoffs.title: Managed service versus custom control
tradeoffs.recommendation: Start with managed primitives where their limits match the access pattern, then isolate replaceable interfaces.
tradeoffs.caution: Provider defaults do not remove the need for quotas, replay, observability, and data lifecycle design.

commonMistakes: Putting all work on the synchronous request path.
Choosing a data store before writing the access patterns and consistency contract.
Ignoring retries, duplicate events, late data, deletion, privacy, or authorization.
Leaving hot partitions, backpressure, stale reads, and recovery unspecified.
Allowing unbounded requests or exports to compete with normal traffic.

followUps.question: What happens when the primary worker is unavailable?
followUps.answer: Acknowledge only after the durable boundary, serve the last acceptable projection, queue retryable work, and replay or reconcile after recovery.

followUps.question: How would you support a tenfold traffic spike?
followUps.answer: Pre-scale partitions, apply admission control and backpressure, isolate hot keys, cache immutable snapshots, and make freshness degradation visible.

followUps.question: How do you verify correctness?
followUps.answer: Use idempotency metrics, version gaps, sampled source-to-projection comparisons, replay tests, and a shadow rebuild before repair.
